records.why: Knock-on: the old text said movement or current flow is essential 'in the same way' for dynamo, bell and generator, and that bell switching is the same as generator magnetisation.
records.old: Movement (or current flow) is essential to electromagnetic action: when it stops, so does the electromagnetic effect — whether in a bicycle dynamo LED, a school electric bell, or the Kericho generator. The bell's electromagnet switching on and off is a miniature, visible demonstration of the same controlled magnetisation and demagnetisation that occurs continuously in industrial generators. This principle — underpinning the KICD key inquiry question 'How is the study of electromagnetic induction important in our daily life?' — powers school bell systems, water pumps on Rift Valley farms, fish-processing equipment in Kisumu, and the national grid that supplies Kenya's homes and industries.
records.new: Two linked ideas: a current can make a magnet (the bell's electromagnet, switched on and off by the make-and-break contact), and a moving magnet can make a current (electromagnetic induction, which is how the dynamo and the Kericho generator work). Together they help answer the KICD key inquiry question 'How is the study of electromagnetic induction important in our daily life?': electromagnets ring school bells, and induction produces the electricity that runs water pumps on Rift Valley farms, fish-processing equipment in Kisumu, and the national grid that supplies Kenya's homes and industries.

records.new: (c) When I closed the circuit, current flowed through the coil around the iron nail and magnetised it, making it an electromagnet. The nail attracted the metal strip (armature), pulling it away from its contact pin and breaking the circuit. With no current, the nail demagnetised and the strip sprang back, closing the circuit again. This repeated make-and-break action produced the ringing. More coil turns or more current made the ring louder and faster. The bell differs from a dynamo: in the bell a current makes a magnet (electromagnetism), while in a dynamo a moving magnet makes a current (electromagnetic induction).

records.why: The CBE level 'Below Expectations' cannot be represented: the contract allows only three level fields (excellent / proficient / developing), and the printed headings are fixed by the template. Suggested: teachers treat any answer below 'Approaches Expectations' as Below Expectations until the contract adds a fourth level.

The Final Explanation (5 parts, including a 10-sentence answer) has no scheduled time: Lesson 8 is only 40 minutes and is already full. Suggested: give the Final Explanation its own 40-minute period after Lesson 8, or set Parts 1-3 as homework and Parts 4-5 in class. The teacher must decide how the school will schedule it; UNIT.totalDuration (600 min) does not include it.

No KICD source is available for this sub-strand. The Grade 10 curriculum PDFs available are Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Mathematics only; the Physics PDF's Strand 3.0 'Electricity and Magnetism' lists 3.1 Electrostatics, 3.2 Current Electricity and 3.3 Introduction to Electronics, with no magnetism or electromagnetic induction sub-strand, and General Science is not covered. So the learning outcomes (a-f), content bullets, key inquiry question, core competencies, values and PCIs recorded in UNIT, and the numbering 'Strand 3.0: Natural Physical Science / Sub-Strand 3.4', could not be checked against KICD wording and were left as they are. Checked internally instead: all six outcomes are taught (a: L1-2, b: L3, c: L4, d: L4, e: L5, f: L6) and assessed in the Final Explanation. Please have a KICD General Science design checked by a teacher.

The electric fence energiser supporting phenomenon (coil and magnetic core give current pulses) is not used in any lesson, so it is listed but never returned to. Suggested: use it in Lesson 7 as an extension, since an energiser's pulsing coil uses the same make-and-break idea as the bell, or drop it from the list.
